title: A pat on the back: complimenting and praising
subtitle: pay a compliment, sing someone's praises, damn with faint praise
summary: Praise people precisely - from paying compliments and heaping praise to back-handed compliments, standing ovations and the informal vocabulary of crawling and sucking up.

lesson.heading: Collocations with compliment
lesson.text: You **pay** someone **a compliment** - you do not give or make one. If you ask for praise in an obvious way, you are **fishing for compliments**. And if something could be read either way, you can choose to **take it as a compliment**.

examples.text: The boss would get better results if she **paid** her staff **compliments** occasionally.
He asked us what we thought of his suit, but he was really only **fishing for compliments**.
**Take it as a compliment** that he feels relaxed enough to fall asleep at your dinner party!
He **complimented me on** my guitar playing.
examples.wrong: He complimented me my guitar playing

lesson.note: The verb compliment is always followed by on.

lesson.heading: Two compliments that are not quite compliments

left.label: back-handed compliment
left.text: Appears positive and negative at the same time, and usually has a malicious intent.
examples: I took it as a **back-handed compliment** when he said I was looking good for my age.

right.label: double-edged compliment
right.text: Also cuts both ways, but is usually made innocently.
examples: She paid me the **double-edged compliment** of saying my driving was pretty good for a beginner.

lesson.heading: Collocations with praise
lesson.text: **Give praise to** is normally kept for a god. An action or a person that deserves praise is **praiseworthy**, and people are **praised for** their actions. Common collocations are **widely/highly praised**, **praised to the skies**, **to sing someone's praises** and **to shower/heap praise on** someone.

examples.text: Her latest novel has been **widely praised** by the critics.
Mrs Carrington is always **praising** her pupils **to the skies**.
At the meeting everyone was **singing your praises**.
He never knows what to say when fans **shower praise on** him.

lesson.heading: Damning with faint praise
lesson.text: To **damn someone with faint praise** is to praise them with such a lack of enthusiasm that you give the impression of actually having rather negative feelings about them. It is a favourite trick of references and reviews.

examples.text: Look at this reference. It's really **damning** the candidate **with faint praise**.
Calling the performance 'perfectly adequate' is **damning it with faint praise**.

lesson.heading: Other expressions relating to praising
rows: pay tribute to
praise; formal
At the memorial service, I paid tribute to his kindness.
give someone a standing ovation
stand up and clap loudly for a long time
At the end of the concert, the audience gave the young pianist a standing ovation.
extol the virtues/benefits of
praise highly; formal
At the conference, the Prime Minister extolled the virtues of the new trade treaty.
be the toast of
be admired for some recent achievement (often used about artists and celebrities)
A few months ago, hardly anyone had heard of her, but now she's the toast of Hollywood.
pat someone on the back / give someone a pat on the back
praise, often children (used mostly metaphorically)
My teacher gave me a pat on the back for my good marks in the maths test.
earn/win plaudits
get positive comments; formal
The exhibition earned plaudits from all the major reviewers.
laud
praise highly in official situations; formal
The Prime Minister has lauded the new peace initiative.
lesson.note: From laud we get laudable (of behaviour) and laudatory (of comments or remarks).

lesson.heading: Praising for your own benefit
lesson.text: These mostly informal expressions imply praising someone in order to get something for yourself: **to flatter**, **to make up to**, **to crawl**, **to suck up to**, **to lick someone's boots**. Someone who behaves like this can be called **smarmy**, **slimy** or **a crawler** (all informal), **a flatterer** (neutral), or **servile** or **obsequious** (more formal).

examples.text: He's always **sucking up to** the boss.
examples.note: informal; He's always flattering the boss is neutral
formal; I wish she wasn't such a crawler is informal

examples.text: When he discovered the size of his mistake, he had to **crawl** to the boss.

lesson.heading: Flattery
lesson.text: **Flatter** also has a more positive use: clothes and light can flatter you. The noun **flattery** turns up in the fixed phrase **Flattery will get you nowhere!**, meaning that insincere praise will not achieve anything.

examples.note: makes her figure look better than it really is

examples.text: There's no point saying how good I am. **Flattery** will get you nowhere!

lesson.text: You pay a compliment but you heap praise - the two nouns take completely different verbs.

exercises.prompt: *A:* Do you like my new hairstyle? *B:* Don't ___ for compliments.
exercises.explanation: To fish for compliments is to invite praise in an obvious way.

exercises.prompt: At the meeting everyone was ___ your praises.
exercises.explanation: To sing someone's praises is to say very good things about them.

exercises.prompt: He's not very good at ___ people compliments.
exercises.explanation: You pay someone a compliment - never give or make one.

exercises.prompt: Mrs Carrington is always praising her pupils ___ the skies.
exercises.explanation: To praise someone to the skies is to praise them enormously.

exercises.prompt: He never knows what to say when fans ___ praise on him.
exercises.explanation: You shower or heap praise on someone.

exercises.prompt: I didn't enjoy the film but it has been very ___ praised by the critics.
exercises.hint: (adverb: by a lot of people / very much)
exercises.explanation: Widely praised and highly praised are the standard collocations.

exercises.prompt: Look at this reference. It's really ___ the candidate with faint praise.
exercises.explanation: To damn someone with faint praise is to praise them so unenthusiastically that you sound negative.

exercises.prompt: Match the beginning of each sentence with its ending.

pairs.left: In the speech, the new manager paid

pairs.right: the virtues of living in the country.
the highest plaudits from the judges.
a pat on the back for her drawings.

pairs.left: The new young Czech player was
pairs.right: the toast of the tennis world.

exercises.prompt: Although she didn't win a prize, the judges were very ___ about her efforts.
exercises.explanation: Complimentary here means full of praise.

exercises.prompt: Jake's a real ___ , so I never take much notice of his compliments.
exercises.explanation: A flatterer praises insincerely; crawler is the informal equivalent.

exercises.prompt: Her actions were foolish but her motives were ___ .
exercises.explanation: Laudable and praiseworthy both mean deserving praise; laudable is a little more formal.

exercises.prompt: Whilst we cannot but ___ the skill of their actions, we must express a certain disapproval of the risks they took.
exercises.explanation: Laud is the formal verb for praising highly in official situations.

exercises.prompt: He said I was looking good for my age. What kind of compliment is that?
exercises.explanation: A back-handed compliment looks positive and negative at once, and tends to be malicious.

options: He complimented me on my guitar playing.
He complimented me my guitar playing.
He complimented me for my guitar playing.
He complimented my guitar playing to me.
exercises.explanation: The verb compliment is followed by on.

exercises.statement: A double-edged compliment is usually made innocently, while a back-handed one tends to be malicious.
exercises.explanation: Correct - both cut two ways, but only the back-handed one is normally intended to wound.

exercises.prompt: Sort these ways of describing someone who praises for their own benefit.
Put this sentence about insincere praise in order.
exercises.answer: There's no point saying how good I am. Flattery will get you nowhere!
exercises.explanation: Flattery will get you nowhere! means insincere praise will not achieve anything.
